title: The Wobbly Baton Race
markdown:
Perrie the rabbit’s nose twitched. Whiskers vibrated with importance. Tomorrow was the Great Meadow Relay, and as captain of the Flutterby Fielders he believed everything must be just right. He was a rabbit who loved his plans. He had planned this relay like a squirrel burying nuts for a hundred winters: the path measured twice, then measured again just to be sure; the start marked with fluffy dandelions like tiny clouds; a chart of who stood where, pinned to a thistle with a polite thorn. And the batons — oh, the batons. He had picked the smoothest oak twigs and polished them until they gleamed like a sleepy badger’s nose. He had lined them by length. He had almost named them, then decided names were a kind of wobble.

“Now, Ruth.” His voice crisp. Ruth, a tiny mouse with dewdrop-gem eyes, was tying a cheerful red ribbon to her tail. “Each runner must know the baton. No fumbling. No mistakes. Understand?”

“Got it! No mistakes!” Tail flick.

He sighed, a tiny puff. She was enthusiastic, and sometimes the enthusiasm wobbled. “Exactly like that. But with the baton. And only when I say.”

“Understood!” She scampered to check the ribbon.

The next morning the meadow buzzed with fizzy-lemonade energy. Dewdrops sparkled like scattered diamonds on the green. Families arrived with picnic crumbs and opinions. Coach Alder, a wise old badger with warm eyes and a rumbling voice, stood near the start as if starts had always belonged to him.

“A fine day for a race, Perrie.”

“Indeed, Coach. The most orderly relay in Sunny Meadow history will begin soon. Everything is precisely as planned.” He puffed his chest and checked the dandelions, which had not moved, which he found comforting.

The first runners lined up. Pipkin the squirrel was there, ready to leap over bushes he had already measured with his eyes. Fiona the fox was ready, moving with a dancer’s grace that made Perrie slightly nervous and also proud. He carefully handed Pipkin the first plain oak baton, still gleaming, still unnamed.

“Remember. A smooth, swift hand-off. No waiting.”

Pipkin nodded, bushy tail twitching. Whistle: toot-toot. A blur. At the exchange Fiona waited. As Pipkin pushed the baton, a tiny delightful pop: a swirl of blue glitter, a mini galaxy. Fiona blinked. “Oh my whiskers. A disco wand!” She took off, a faint shimmer in the air.

Next, Meilyr the badger cub, a bit clumsy, strong. Fiona handed him the baton. It did not just glitter. Poof: a magnificent emerald-green feather unfurled, tickling his nose. He giggled, a happy rumble. “Whee!” He flapped the feather with glee. Paws like mittens; the feather felt light enough to fly.

Perrie watched, ears drooping. Plain oak decorating itself. Not the plan. Not order.

Ruth took the baton from Meilyr. Twirl: tiny tinkling bells. She skipped, ribbon bobbing. “Ding-a-ling! A marching band!” Tiny paws flying.

Whiskers drooped further. A proper relay turning into a parade of sparkly feathery jingly nonsense. Tremor in the paws, up to the twitching nose, tight in the tummy. He wanted neat and predictable. Not this.

He watched, despite himself, as the batons kept changing as if the meadow had opinions about oak. One grew a vine of cheerful daisies that nodded in time with the runner’s paws. Another decided to wrap itself in rainbow ribbon and refused to be unwrapped. A third briefly smelled of honey, which was not decoration but did not help Perrie’s mood. The last, held by his younger sister Lily, who was usually quite shy and walked with her head down, grew a fuzzy friendly pom-pom at the end. Lily let out a surprising giggle. She bounced the pom-pom as she ran, a bright smile spreading, the pom-pom like a happy friend who had been waiting all season for a job.

Finish line in sight. Heart a drum. He had failed. Orderly relay, colourful mess.

Then he saw it. The meadow was not only cheering; it was giggling. Runners not only running; full of joy. Pipkin, glitter, more confident than ever. Fiona, disco wand, seeming to float. Meilyr, feather high, proud. Ruth, jingle-bells, a blur of happy energy. Lily, pom-pom bouncing, a new bounce, smile to her ears.

They crossed not in one perfect moment but in a delightful jumble. Astonishing part: not a single drop. Each seemed faster, more heart, because the unique baton made them feel special, seen.

Coach Alder ambled over, eyes twinkling. “Quite a relay.”

Perrie looked at happy slightly messy runners, smiles like little suns. Warmth on fur, happy chatter, sweet meadow flowers.

“It wasn’t proper,” he admitted, ears still a little low.

“Sometimes proper is just one way. Sometimes letting everyone be a little bit them — quirks, sparkles — is the best way to have fun, and to truly win.”

Perrie looked at his own baton. In the joyful chaos it had acquired a charming sunflower. He had been so busy about order he had forgotten joy. Friends’ faces alight with pride in their dazzling individual sticks. A real smile chased the tightness away.

“Yes, Coach. I think you’re right.” The sunflower felt good, warm, cheerful. The Great Meadow Relay had not been proper. It had been something better. Confidence of a new kind: let a little sparkle and a lot of fun lead. It felt, he decided, even better than perfect.

After the jumble at the line there were drinks of stream-water and a great deal of comparing decorations, as if the batons had become members of the team. Pipkin demonstrated the glitter swirl twice. Fiona taught Lily a twirl that did not drop the pom-pom. Meilyr sneezed when the feather found his nose again, and everyone counted that as a cheer.

He logged dandelion-start / glitter-pop / feather-bells-pompom / sunflower finish in the team book, left the measuring string coiled and unused beside the thistle chart, and let Ruth retie her ribbon while Meilyr practised a victory flap that knocked over nothing important. Coach Alder rumbled approval. Perrie, captain of plans, ran the last stretch again for the fun of the jingle, which was not on any list and did not need to be. The sunflower, warm in his paw, agreed.
